title: Pliny's Letters: Eruption of Mt. Vesuvius

guide.summary: Unit 2 covers Pliny the Younger's two letters to the historian Tacitus about the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE: Letter 6.16 on the death of his uncle, Pliny the Elder, and Letter 6.20 on his own and his mother's escape from Misenum.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Pliny the Younger (c. 61–c. 113 CE), a senator and lawyer, published carefully crafted letters (Epistulae) that present a polished self-image. Tacitus, writing his Histories, asked Pliny how his uncle died so he could record it for posterity; Pliny's letters combine eyewitness detail, admiration for his uncle, and literary art. Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic Natural History, commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum on the Bay of Naples. The eruption of 79 CE buried Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Stabiae.

sections.heading: Letter 6.16: the uncle
sections.body: The elder Pliny sees a strange cloud rising from a mountain (later known to be Vesuvius), shaped like an umbrella pine. A scholar's curiosity makes him prepare a light boat to investigate, but a message from Rectina, a woman trapped near the mountain, turns the trip into a rescue with warships (quadriremes). As ash and pumice fall and the helmsman urges retreat, he declares 'Fortes fortuna iuvat' and heads for his friend Pomponianus at Stabiae. There he calmly bathes, dines, and sleeps to reassure the frightened household. As the buildings shake, the group goes out with pillows tied on their heads for protection. On the shore, he collapses and dies, apparently overcome by fumes; his body is later found intact, looking more like a man asleep than dead. Pliny portrays him as courageous, curious, and selfless, a model of Roman virtus and constantia.

sections.heading: Letter 6.20: the nephew
sections.body: Seventeen-year-old Pliny stays at Misenum reading Livy as earthquakes intensify, then flees with his mother amid panicking crowds. A dark cloud descends; the darkness is like that of a closed room with the lamp put out. His mother urges him to save himself and leave her behind; he refuses and helps her along. He contrasts his own fear with his calm, and reflects that he took comfort in the belief that he was dying with the whole world. Pliny ends by noting that these details are not worthy of history but that Tacitus may use them as he likes, a modest pose that also showcases his literary skill. Sight passages like the one above test similar vocabulary of panic, flight, and natural disaster.

keyTakeaways: Pliny the Elder: fleet commander at Misenum, author of Natural History.
Pine-shaped cloud; Rectina's plea; 'Fortes fortuna iuvat'.
Calm at Stabiae; death on the shore.
Young Pliny refuses to abandon his mother.
commonMistakes: Confusing the uncle (Elder) with the nephew (Younger).
Forgetting the letters' audience (Tacitus) and purpose.
Treating Pliny's narrative as neutral reporting.
Mixing up Misenum (the fleet) and Stabiae (Pomponianus).
examTips: Know the sequence of events in both letters.
Connect details to virtues (virtus, pietas, constantia).

practice.prompt: Answer the questions about the sight passage above.

parts.prompt: What contrast does alii ... alii create?
Identify the tense and mood of amiserat and translate the clause.
Identify the form and use of sedens.
Identify the form of terribiliorem and translate the final sentence.

rubric.description: multa aedificia corruerunt: many buildings collapsed.
se proripuerunt: they rushed out / hurled themselves into the streets.
alii ... alii: some ... others; contrasts two reactions.
qui patrem amiserat: pluperfect indicative, 'who had lost his father'.
sedens: present active participle modifying puer, 'sitting'.
nullum diem ... terribiliorem: comparative adjective; 'no day had ever been more terrible'.

practice.sampleResponse:
1. Many buildings collapsed (multa aedificia corruerunt).
2. Se proripuerunt means 'they rushed out' into the streets; the reflexive emphasizes frantic, headlong movement.
3. Alii... alii means 'some... others' and shows the citizens' different responses: prayer and searching for family.
4. Amiserat is pluperfect indicative: 'who had lost his father', an action before the boy wept.
5. Sedens is a present active participle modifying puer: 'sitting' under the tree.
6. Terribiliorem is a comparative adjective agreeing with diem: they said that no day had ever been more terrible.
